title: Play to Your Strengths
hook: Harlan can promise white-glove service, but the call queue knows what the company can really do.
counterintuition: Most teams list strengths they admire. Strategy needs capabilities that fit the chosen way to win. A strength that does not support the edge can become expensive pride. Instead, the useful strength is the one that helps the chosen promise survive pressure.
tryThisNow: Take the plan closest to your hand and underline the sentence that claims to be a choice. Beside it, write what it would make you stop doing this week.
keyTakeaway: Capabilities matter when they reinforce the chosen edge, so the hard work is testing which strengths are real, which are missing, and which no longer fit.

breakdown.fastRead:
Harlan listens to hold music at 4:12 p.m. beside the support floor. The strategy says white-glove service. The queue says forty-three calls waiting.

Strength is not what the company praises in itself. Strength is what the chosen way to win requires and the system can deliver again tomorrow.

If the promise needs a capability the team does not have, the promise is not strategic. It is a future apology.
breakdown.deepRead:
Sonal stands in a school kitchen with a farm-to-table menu and two dented steam tables. The district wants fresh lunches. The cooks are skilled, but deliveries arrive late and knives are shared across three prep stations. The capability gap is not passion. It is cold-chain timing, prep space, and purchasing discipline.

Play to your strengths does not mean do what you already like. It means build the few capabilities that make the chosen edge believable. Sometimes the strength exists. Sometimes it must be built. Sometimes an old strength must lose status because the strategy changed.

Picture Rivka in a pharmacy stockroom. Everyone praises her head pharmacist, who remembers every customer. The chosen edge is same-day chronic refill reliability. One star memory cannot carry that. The system needs refill reminders, supplier checks, and technician handoffs.

The limit is honesty. A team can love a strength that no longer matters. Strategy asks fit, not nostalgia.

A hotel manager can praise the staff for friendliness, and the praise may be true. If the strategy is fastest check-in for late business travelers, friendliness needs help from mobile keys, clean room status, and a night desk script that solves problems in minutes. The admired trait becomes strategic only when it is joined to the capabilities the promise needs.
breakdown.fullRead:
Petrina walks through a fulfillment aisle at 6:08 a.m., touching the blue bins that hold premium gift orders. The new strategy promises custom packaging shipped within twenty-four hours. Marketing loves the phrase. The floor has one label printer, two seasonal temps, and no quality check after ribbon tying. Petrina can see the promise becoming a stack of refunds.

Capabilities are the skills, processes, tools, and habits that let a strategy happen repeatedly. They are not a list of virtues. Friendly culture, smart people, hard work, and good taste are useful only when they connect to the chosen edge. If the edge is custom speed, the system needs fast art approval, stocked materials, clean handoffs, and a check that catches wrong notes before packing.

Jovana gets the same lesson in a clinic. The clinic wants to win with warm same-day care for working parents. The doctor is excellent, but the phones open at 9:00, after many parents are already on shift. The needed capability is not more medical skill. It is early triage, text booking, and a nurse protocol that clears simple visits before lunch. The admired strength remains real. It is just not enough.

Nakul shows the trap inside personal growth. He wants to build a freelance design practice and lists his strengths: taste, patience, curiosity, craft. The clients who would pay need fast landing pages for small launches. He has to build quoting, templates, revision rules, and delivery rhythm. Taste helps. The business depends on repeatable throughput.

A capability choice has two sides. First, protect what truly supports the edge. Second, stop funding strengths that only feel prestigious. The old excellence may be beautiful and still wrong for the new game.

Before you praise a strength, ask what promise it helps you keep under pressure. If no customer would notice its absence, it may be a hobby wearing a strategy badge.

Capabilities also have to reinforce one another. A fast quote process without fast material supply creates a new bottleneck. A skilled clinician without early triage leaves working parents stuck on hold. A brilliant designer without revision rules spends taste on endless loops. The system matters because customers experience the chain, not the strongest link in isolation.

This is where pride can get expensive. Leaders often protect a capability because it built the old reputation. The company may still be good at it. The question is whether it supports the current edge. If it does not, the team has to decide how much status, money, and leadership time it should keep.

Build capability work into the calendar. Pick one weak link that blocks the promise, assign an owner, and review evidence of improvement every week. A capability that nobody practices, funds, or checks is only a hope with a better label.

examples.title: Harlan listens to forty-three calls under the service poster

planSpec.requiredBeat: white-glove claim meets call queue reality

examples.scenario: Harlan stands at 4:12 p.m. under a poster that says white-glove service while the support screen shows forty-three calls waiting. A sales deck on his tablet promises every premium account a named contact. The best agents are already handling escalations, and two new hires are reading scripts. He can approve the promise for Monday's pitch or stop the launch until the support system can carry it.
examples.whatToDo: Audit the promise against real support capacity. Delay or narrow the offer until staffing, routing, and account ownership can repeat the service on a bad afternoon.
examples.whyItMatters: A capability claim is only true when the floor can deliver it under load. Harlan needs the strategy to fit what the system can actually do.

examples.title: Sonal finds the farm menu blocked by steam tables

planSpec.requiredBeat: passion is not the capability gap

examples.scenario: Sonal stands in the school kitchen at 1:44 p.m., scraping roasted carrots from a dented steam table. The farm-to-table pilot had beautiful posters and cooks who cared. It also had late deliveries, one prep sink, and knives shared between salad and hot lunch. She writes failed because staff resisted, then crosses it out. The staff wanted it. The capability system did not.
examples.whatToDo: Map the capabilities the fresh menu requires: delivery timing, prep space, knife stations, and purchasing rules. Build those before judging the cooks.
examples.whyItMatters: The wrong postmortem blames attitude and misses the system. Sonal needs to know which capabilities make the chosen lunch promise possible.

examples.title: Rivka tells the owner one pharmacist is not a system

planSpec.requiredBeat: one star employee cannot carry same-day refill edge

examples.scenario: Rivka is in the pharmacy stockroom at 7:05 p.m., counting blister packs while the owner praises Tomer at the front counter. "He remembers everyone," the owner says. Rivka points to three refill slips clipped to an empty bin. "Our promise is same-day chronic refills," she says. "Tomer's memory is a gift, but what happens on his day off?" The refrigerator hum fills the pause.
examples.whatToDo: Turn the admired employee skill into a repeatable system: reminders, stock checks, technician handoffs, and clear backup rules.
examples.whyItMatters: A star can hide weakness for a while. The strategy needs a capability that survives vacation, sickness, and the next busy Thursday.

examples.title: Petrina sees ribbon tying break the custom-shipping promise

planSpec.requiredBeat: custom speed requires new operational capabilities

examples.scenario: Petrina predicted the premium gift line could ship custom boxes within twenty-four hours. At 6:08 a.m., she walks the fulfillment aisle and watches one temp hunt for ivory ribbon while another waits for the only label printer. A wrong gift note sits in the discard tray. The promise is not blocked by demand. It is blocked by missing capabilities she can name.
examples.whatToDo: List the exact capabilities the promise needs and build the first weak one before selling more volume. Start with materials, label flow, and note checks.
examples.whyItMatters: The edge is not custom packaging in a phrase. It is a set of small abilities that must work in order when orders pile up.

examples.title: Jovana opens the clinic phones before the first shift change
examples.scenario: At 8:02 a.m., Jovana watches three missed calls blink on the clinic phone while parents line up at the factory gate across the street. The clinic used to praise its excellent doctor and open phones at nine. After she names working-parent same-day care as the edge, the phones open at seven-thirty, a nurse triages simple cases, and the first text confirmations go out before shift change.
examples.whatToDo: Build the capabilities around the chosen parent need, not around the clinic's old pride. Early phones and triage make the promise real.
examples.whyItMatters: Medical skill still matters, but the chosen edge depends on access at the hour parents can use it. The capability must match the promise.

examples.title: Nakul times the landing-page handoff at the laundromat

planSpec.requiredBeat: taste alone does not deliver fast launch pages

examples.scenario: Nakul sits in a laundromat at 9:36 p.m. with a client text asking if the landing page can go live by Friday. His notebook lists strengths: taste, patience, curiosity. The washer thumps behind him. None of those words tells him how to quote, collect copy, limit revisions, or hand off files. He draws four boxes across the page and starts building the delivery system.
examples.whatToDo: Convert broad strengths into the few capabilities the offer needs: quote, copy intake, revision limit, and launch handoff. Practice those until delivery is repeatable.
examples.whyItMatters: Taste helps Nakul win only when clients receive the page on time. The real strength is the system that turns taste into a kept promise.

questions.prompt: A manager is staring at a planning slide with eight equal priorities and one budget line already cut. The team wants language that keeps every group happy before the Thursday review. Which action best applies the move?
choices: Force the slide to name the one choice that decides the rest.
Add a sentence saying all priorities remain important.
Delay the review until every leader has edited the slide.
questions.explanation: The right move makes the choice visible. A strategy that protects every claim cannot guide scarce money or attention.

questions.prompt: A teacher is picking projects for a six-week unit. Three options are useful, but only one fits the students she most wants to serve this term. What should she do first?
choices: Run all three as shorter projects.
Choose the project that fits the chosen students and let the others wait.
Ask students to vote without naming the learning target.
questions.explanation: The useful option is not always the strategic option. Fit to the chosen aim should lead the decision.

questions.prompt: A founder has a new offer, a thin cash balance, and two customer groups asking for different features by Friday. Which response best keeps the strategy coherent?
choices: Promise both groups a lighter version.
Build the feature requested by the louder group.
Pick the customer group tied to the win and say no to the other request.
questions.explanation: The move protects the chosen game. Saying yes to the wrong buyer can spend the same resources while weakening the path to win.

questions.prompt: A clinic team notices its dashboard is full of green marks, but patients in the chosen service line still wait too long. Which action fits the lesson?
choices: Change the measure so it tracks the wait that decides the chosen service line.
Celebrate the green dashboard to keep morale high.
Add a second dashboard for every department.
questions.explanation: Measures should support the actual choice. A green report that misses the chosen result trains the team to drift politely.

questions.prompt: A parent is helping a teenager plan summer activities. The list has sports, coding, travel, work, and test prep, all marked urgent. What is the best next move?
choices: Rank the activities by how impressive they sound.
Name the one summer outcome that should lead the schedule.
Keep all activities and shorten sleep for two weeks.
questions.explanation: A clear leading aim makes the rest easier to sort. Without it, every good option claims the same space.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit board wants to serve seniors, new immigrants, artists, and local schools with one small grant. Which plan best follows the move?
choices: Split the grant into four equal mini-programs.
Use the grant on the group with the loudest advocate.
Choose one audience and design the program to win trust there first.
questions.explanation: Small resources need a field. Equal spread can feel fair while making the work too weak for anyone.

questions.prompt: A restaurant owner is choosing between faster lunch service, a deeper dinner menu, and catering. The kitchen can support only one new habit this month. What should she do?
choices: Choose the habit that reinforces the desired position with customers.
Try all three and review after staff burn out.
Let each shift choose its own priority.
questions.explanation: The best action reinforces the same edge. A kitchen cannot learn three different games at once.

questions.prompt: A student group has survey data, interview notes, and pricing guesses, but nobody has written the actual options on the wall. Which move should come next?
choices: Collect more survey answers before speaking.
Write two or three real options and use the evidence to test them.
Pick the safest option because it has fewer objections.
questions.explanation: Evidence needs options to judge. More facts do not help until the group names the paths it might take.

questions.prompt: A designer wants confidence before narrowing a product concept. She can test one assumption with five users tomorrow. Which plan best fits the move?
choices: Wait until the full prototype is polished.
Ask friends which concept sounds more exciting.
Test the assumption that would kill the concept if it fails.
questions.explanation: The strongest test puts pressure on the condition that carries the decision. It improves the odds faster than broad reassurance.

reviewCards.front: You see a plan with many good options and no lead choice. What question should you ask first?
reviewCards.back: Ask which result or customer is allowed to decide the next tradeoff. The answer should make at least one attractive option fall behind.

reviewCards.front: A team says every priority matters equally. How do you test whether play to your strengths is real?
reviewCards.back: Look for a resource shift, a narrower field, or a changed routine. If nothing changes after the words are approved, the choice is still soft.

reviewCards.front: A colleague objects that narrowing the plan feels risky. What answer keeps the work practical?
reviewCards.back: Say that narrowing is not about being small. It is about putting force behind the field where the team has the best chance to win.

reviewCards.front: You have one week before a review and too many claims in the plan. What should be on your scratch pad?
reviewCards.back: Write the chosen win, field, edge, needed capabilities, and management checks. Then mark any claim that does not support that chain.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is capability fit. You learn to test strengths against the chosen edge and build the few missing abilities that matter most.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a meeting starts with a list of equal priorities, then ask which one choice should receive money, people, or calendar time first.
If you add a new routine, then name the one health result it serves and remove one routine that does not help that result this month.
If your weekend plan has more than three serious goals, then choose the one goal that would make Sunday night feel won and schedule it first.
If a shared plan is getting broad and polite, then ask what both of you are willing to stop doing so the chosen aim has room.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the next planning conversation, write one promised edge, the three capabilities it requires, and the weakest capability you can improve this week. Circle the one answer that should force a real tradeoff, then bring only that circled choice to the room.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For seven days, keep a one-page choice log. Each time a plan grows wider, write the choice, the option you refused, and what changed because you refused it.
